query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory HEA the unusual and seemingly disconnected behaviors observed in creep at high temperature, microhardness after cold rolling, and modulus changes with temperature all originate from thermally induced lattice distortions and residual stresses. These stresses arise because microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., transient precipitates from aging and dislocation networks from cold rolling) have different thermal expansion behavior than the surrounding matrix. The resulting thermal expansion mismatch during cooling or subsequent heating creates internal stresses that modulate dislocation mobility and interatomic spacing, thereby unifying the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic responses.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy in a homogenized as-cast state with minimal initial microsegregation and low dislocation density.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal treatments to create two conditions: (a) an aged condition (600–800 °C) that induces microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., precipitate formation) and higher dislocation density via subsequent cold rolling, and (b) a homogenized condition achieved by rapid annealing to minimize compositional segregation and microstructural heterogeneity. Compare their mechanical responses.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted in inert atmosphere over a wide temperature range: elastic modulus measured from 293 K to 1100 K, tensile creep testing at 1250 °C, and microhardness measurements performed on cold-rolled samples. The comparison is controlled so that the only variable is the degree of microstructural heterogeneity and associated residual stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual thermal stresses and lattice distortions generated by the thermal expansion mismatch between heterogeneously formed microstructural features (such as precipitates and dislocation networks) and the surrounding matrix.
generation.mechanism: During thermal processing and subsequent cooling, regions that develop precipitates or receive heavy cold work exhibit a different thermal expansion coefficient compared to the matrix. This mismatch creates intrinsic residual stresses that alter the potential energy landscape for dislocation motion as well as interatomic distances. Consequently, these internal stresses control the observed high-temperature creep resistance, influence the elastic modulus over temperature, and contribute to higher hardness after cold rolling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that are purposefully aged (600–800 °C) to promote microstructural heterogeneity and then cold rolled will show higher residual stresses (as measured by X‐ray diffraction) along with increased yield strength and creep resistance at 1250 °C and anomalous elastic modulus trends (deviating more from the mixture rule) compared to homogenized samples. In contrast, homogenized samples with minimal heterogeneity and residual stress should show lower strength and more conventional temperature dependence of elastic moduli.
generation.baseline: The homogenized HfNbTaTiZr alloy with minimal aging-induced heterogeneity and low dislocation density (minimizing residual thermal stresses).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to operate across a wide temperature span: from room temperature up to 1250 °C, specifically becoming evident in samples aged between 600 °C and 800 °C and then cold worked. Deviations in elastic modulus are observable between 293 K and 1100 K, and creep behavior is prominent at 1250 °C.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative link between thermally induced residual stresses and mechanical behavior is supported by previous observations, their exact quantitative contributions relative to intrinsic atomic bonding or dislocation properties remain uncertain and require further detailed microstructural and stress analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set is subjected to a homogenization treatment (rapid annealing to reduce heterogeneity) and the other is aged at 600–800 °C to induce precipitate formation followed by controlled cold rolling. Keep all other processing parameters constant to isolate the effect of microstructural heterogeneity and the associated residual stresses.
measurements: X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction for mapping residual stress levels and lattice distortions
Elastic modulus measurements over the range 293–1100 K
TEM analysis for dislocation density and precipitate characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged, heterogeneous samples do not exhibit significantly higher residual stresses and corresponding improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, or altered elastic modulus trends compared to the homogenized baseline, then the hypothesis that thermal expansion mismatch–induced residual stresses govern the unified mechanical behavior is falsified.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen

Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.

Conclusions: Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived
